idea-plugin.name: Maven Prime
idea-plugin.description:
Everything you expect from a Maven plugin, plus the answers none of them give you. Run and debug any goal, run your tests the way Maven runs them, win any dependency argument. Then find out why the build is slow, where a version really came from, and what is rotting in your local repository.

  • Goals you save once, each one a real IDE action with its own shortcut.
  • Tests run and debugged through Maven, reported in the IDE test tree.
  • Dependency Analyzer on the tree the IDE already resolved: conflicts, every path, and why.
  • Effective values inline: every ${property} and inherited version, in the POM.
  • Profiler: which plugin, goal or module the build time went to, and which one is worth fixing.
  • Downloads: how much of the build was the network, and which repository it waited on.
  • Model: every version, plugin and property beside the POM that really set it.
  • Repository: what is missing, half-downloaded or negatively cached in ~/.m2.
  • Build context shared with your team, with your own machine always winning.
  • Maven Daemon found or installed for you, and options rendered for Maven 3, 4 or mvnd.

Run and debug any goal, on the module you are already in

One popup, from the editor or the project tree, already pointed at the right module. Save the goals you keep retyping: each one becomes a real IDE action, so it gets its own keyboard shortcut and its own toolbar button. A saved goal carries its own profiles, properties, options, JRE and Maven version, so the fast build and the thorough one live side by side.

  • Run icons in the gutter of pom.xml: the whole module, one plugin, one execution.
  • Run a goal before any run configuration launches, as a before-launch step.
  • Force Clean, skip tests and offline are toggles, not edits to the goals you saved.
  • Colored Maven output. Maven gives up on color inside an IDE; Maven Prime asks for it anyway.

Run and debug your tests through Maven

Run one test method or one test class the way Maven will run it in CI, and read the result in the IDE test tree instead of scrolling console output. Debug attaches to the JVMs that Surefire forks, so a breakpoint inside the test is actually hit.

Win the dependency argument

The analyzer opens on the pom.xml you are reading, in the editor, on the tree the IDE has already resolved, so there is nothing to wait for. It shows which versions clashed, which one won, and every path that drags an artifact in.

  • Every path also says why it was kept or dropped: omitted for conflict, managed by dependency management, duplicate, excluded. Seeing the paths is not the same as knowing the reason.
  • Exclude the one you do not want and Maven Prime writes it into the declaration that actually causes it. When that declaration is inherited, it tells you where, instead of quietly changing every module that inherits it.
  • Jump from any artifact straight into your local repository, and back again.
  • Sort by size on disk, when you need to know what made the build heavy.

That is the part you already expect. Here is the rest.

Know why the build is slow

Per-module times tell you nothing about a parallel build. Maven Prime measures the build from the inside and lays it out as a timeline, one lane per build thread Maven really used, showing where a thread sat with nothing to run and which module it was waiting for.

The same timings regroup by plugin, goal or lifecycle phase, so you can ask which plugin costs you the most across the whole reactor instead of which single module was slowest. And every module carries what the build would save if it took no time at all: a module off the critical path saves nothing however long it took, so you stop optimising the one that was never the problem.

See what the build spent on the network

Maven prints a line per file and never a total, so the time a build waits on downloads is invisible. Maven Prime totals it: how long the build was downloading, how much came down, and which repository it came from. Against a cold local repository that can be almost the whole build.

Every ${property} resolved, in the POM you are reading

A placeholder shows what the effective model actually resolved it to, right beside it, and not only inside a version tag. A dependency or plugin with no version shows the one it inherits from dependency or plugin management. Click a value and the file that decided it opens on the line, parent POMs included. No build to run, no tab to open, no guessing which ancestor won.

Know where a version came from

Every dependency, every plugin and every property, beside the POM that really set it. Parents included, even the ones that exist only in your local repository. One double-click and you are looking at the line.

One build context, honored everywhere

Profiles, properties and the Maven environment in one place, applied to every run. Flip a profile and the effective model reloads itself, so what the IDE resolves is what your next build will really do.

Keep that context in the repository and the whole team has it on the next pull. Your own changes always win, so a shared setup never fights your machine, and nothing from a repository applies until you trust it.

A local repository you can trust

Artifacts that were never downloaded, that answered 404 everywhere, or that died halfway. Which repositories were tried, and when. Sources and javadoc that are not really there. And when Maven has cached a failure and refuses to retry, clear it for that one artifact instead of deleting your local repository and downloading the internet again.

  • Any artifact in your local repository, straight from Search Everywhere.
  • Newer published versions show up on their own: no button, no request, no waiting.
  • Credentials for the repository that refused you, kept in the IDE password safe.

Builds that start instantly

The Maven Daemon keeps the JVM warm between builds. Maven Prime finds the one you have or installs one for you, keeps the daemons in check, and never sends an option the Maven you picked cannot run: it drops it and tells you which one.

And the small things you keep wishing for

  • Add as Dependency writes the element into the module POM for you.
  • Any dependency copied as ready-to-paste XML, or as plain coordinates.
  • Intentions on the POM: analyze an artifact, go to the version that decided it, exclude it.
  • Options rendered for the Maven that will really run it, whether that is Maven 3, Maven 4 or mvnd.
  • The recent builds are kept, not only the last one, so the run that failed differently is one pick away instead of another rerun.
  • The goals you save and the whole build context travel in one file at the root of the repository.

Free, and open source under Apache 2.0.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.3.0
  • Profiler: the timings now group by plugin, goal, phase or build thread, not only by module. Grouping by plugin answers what the old table could not ask: which plugin costs you the most across the whole reactor, rather than which single module was slowest. Sort by duration, by the order the build ran things in, or by name, and narrow the rows by typing.
  • Worth speeding up: each module now carries what the build would save if that module took no time at all. A module off the critical path saves nothing however long it took, so the list stays short even when the build does not, and you stop optimising the module that was never the problem.
  • Downloads: Maven prints a line per file and never a total, so the time a build spends waiting on the network is invisible. The profiler now shows how long the build was downloading, how much came down and which repository it came from. Against a cold local repository that can be almost the whole build.
  • The timeline lanes are the build threads Maven really used, instead of a guess made from which modules happened to overlap. Where a thread sat with nothing to run, the timeline draws the gap and names the module it was waiting for.
  • Where the Build Time Went no longer repeats itself. A single-module build used to show the same number on five rows and then advise running it with -T 1 to bring six seconds down to six seconds. Rows that add nothing are left out, and a thread count is suggested only where more threads could actually help.
  • Every figure explains itself. Hover the ? beside a number, or hover a column header, to find out what Duration, Wall Clock or Payoff mean without leaving the tab.
  • Hover the profiler summary for the goals that produced the numbers you are reading, and the build drop-down to tell one recorded run from another.
  • Dependency Analyzer opens with the tree and the paths side by side instead of one above the other, which is the shape most screens have room for. The button that switches between the two now says which layout it gives you.
1.2.0
  • Profiler: Open in Editor opens the profiler as an editor tab, where the timeline gets the full width of the window instead of a narrow column beside your code.
  • Turn on Report a build whose time can be recovered and a build that could have been faster says so when it finishes, with a link straight to the profiler. It is off until you turn it on, and it stays quiet unless there are at least ten seconds and a fifth of the build to win back.
  • The verdict under the timeline no longer contradicts itself on a wide build. It used to say a build ran 37 modules at once and, in the same sentence, that only 8 were allowed.
  • A build held back by its dependencies no longer shows the same number twice, once as time more threads would win back and once as overhead.
  • Large builds are no longer reported as measured only in part.
  • Model: the value shown beside a ${property} follows the POM. Change a version property and the value moves with the next Maven reload, instead of staying on what it was the last time the model was read.
  • The Model tab is marked when the POMs have changed since the model was read, so you can tell from any tab that what it shows is behind.
  • Settings: choose how many past runs the Model, Profiler and Repository drop-downs keep. Twenty, as before, unless you change it.
1.1.2
  • Build context: a property marked Apply to the IDE Maven import no longer reaches the importer on its own. Apply to the IDE Maven Import on the Build Context properties toolbar writes the marked properties, and takes back exactly what it wrote, so whatever you typed into the importer VM options yourself stays there.
  • The two markers an earlier version fenced its region with reached the importer JVM as real -D definitions. They are taken out of the field the first time this version reads it.
  • Profiles: a profile that a module brings in, or takes away, appears and disappears as soon as the import finishes, in the profiles popup as well as in the tool window.
  • The profiles popup keeps the size you drag it to and treats it as a minimum: a longer name or one more row widens it, a shorter list leaves it as it is.
  • A finished import no longer pushes the profiles back into the IDE and starts a second one.
1.1.1
  • Profiler: the timeline no longer paints its bars over the rest of the tool window on builds with more modules running at once than fit on screen, or at any zoom past the whole build.
1.1.0
  • Profiler: every bar carries the duration of the module it stands for, and clicking a bar selects that module in the details below. Bars too short to aim at are easier to hit.
  • Goals: clone a saved goal instead of retyping it.
  • .mavenprime.json is never written on your behalf. Create it when you want to share the goals and build context you have, from the Maven settings wheel or the Maven Prime settings.
  • Until that file exists, your goals and build context stay with the project under .idea. Wherever the file is present, it is the one that counts.
  • A .mavenprime.json written by a newer Maven Prime is read as far as this one can read it, and is never written over.
  • Daemons: Remove deletes the daemon Maven Prime downloaded rather than letting it return on the next scan. A daemon you installed yourself is left where it is.
  • The tool window follows the editor and the project tree without holding the UI thread.
1.0.0
  • Initial release.
